source_text: Ἐπειδὴ ὁρῶ, κράτιστε Διόγνητε, ὑπερεσπουδακότα σε τὴν θεοσέβειαν τῶν Χριστιανῶν μαθεῖν καὶ πάνυ σαφῶς καὶ ἐπιμελῶς πυνθανόμενον περὶ αὐτῶν, τίνι τε θεῷ πεποιθότες καὶ πῶς θρησκεύοντες αὐτὸν τόν τε κόσμον ὑπερορῶσι πάντες καὶ θανάτου καταφρονοῦσι καὶ οὔτε τοὺς νομιζομένους ὑπὸ τῶν Ἑλλήνων θεοὺς λογίζονται οὔτε τὴν Ἰουδαίων δεισιδαιμονίαν φυλάσσουσι, καὶ τίνα τὴν φιλοστοργίαν ἔχουσι πρὸς ἀλλήλους, καὶ τί δή ποτε καινὸν τοῦτο γένος ἢ ἐπιτήδευμα εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸν βίον νῦν καὶ οὐ πρότερον: ἀποδέχομαί γε τῆς προθυμίας σε ταύτης καὶ παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ, τοῦ καὶ τὸ λέγειν καὶ τὸ ἀκούειν ἡμῖν χορηγοῦντος, αἰτοῦμαι δοθῆναι ἐμοὶ μὲν εἰπεῖν οὕτως, ὡς μάλιστα ἂν ἀκούσαντά σε βελτίω γενέσθαι, σοί τε οὕτως ἀκοῦσαι, ὡς μὴ λυπηθῆναι τὸν εἰπόντα.
thought_title: Opening address and request for effective speech
orientation: The author opens the letter by addressing Diognetus, a distinguished pagan who has eagerly asked to learn about the Christians' piety.
pass_a_gloss: Since I see, [most] excellent Diognetus, [that] you have been exceedingly eager to learn the piety of the Christians and [are] very clearly and carefully inquiring about them, [namely] in what God [they] have trusted and how [they] worship him, [that] they all both despise the world and scorn death, and neither regard the gods considered by the Greeks [as gods] nor keep the superstition of the Jews, and what [the] affection [is that] they have toward one another, and why ever [this] new race or practice has entered into [the] life now and not before: I welcome indeed this eagerness of yours, and from God, the [one] who supplies to us both the speaking and the hearing, I ask [that it] be given to me on the one hand to speak in such a way, as especially [that] you having heard [it] might become better, and to you on the other hand to hear in such a way, as [that] the [one] having spoken might not be grieved.

choices.why: The glossary fixes 'piety' for θεοσέβεια, the reverent worship of God that Diognetus wants to learn about.
The glossary fixes 'superstition' for the negative Jewish observance the Christians reject.
A standard honorific address to a distinguished person; 'most excellent' preserves the superlative force.
The pair contrasts an ethnic identity with a way of life; 'race' and 'practice' keep both senses distinct.
The verb expresses warm approval of Diognetus's eagerness; 'welcome' captures the receptive tone.
The verb means to furnish or provide generously; 'supplies' fits God as the giver of both speaking and hearing.

pass_b_english: I see, most excellent Diognetus, how eager you are to learn the piety of the Christians. You are asking about them with great clarity and care. What God have they trusted? How do they worship him? Why do all of them despise the world and scorn death? Why do they neither regard the gods recognized by the Greeks nor keep the superstition of the Jews? What affection do they have for one another? And why has this new way of life appeared now and not before? I welcome your eagerness. I ask God, who supplies us with both speaking and hearing, to grant me to speak in such a way that you who hear may become better, and to grant you to hear in such a way that the one who speaks may not be grieved.

problems.quote: and why this new race or practice has entered life now and not before
problems.source_quote: καὶ τί δή ποτε καινὸν τοῦτο γένος ἢ ἐπιτήδευμα εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸν βίον νῦν καὶ οὐ πρότερον
problems.why: Greek asks what new kind/practice has entered, not why.
problems.fix: and what new kind or practice has entered life now and not before
problems.ruling: τί δή ποτε asks 'what' new race/practice entered life, not 'why'; translator changes the question's content.

problems.quote: And I ask God, who supplies us with both speaking and hearing
problems.source_quote: ἀποδέχομαί γε τῆς προθυμίας σου ταύτης καὶ παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ, τοῦ καὶ τὸ λέγειν καὶ τὸ ἀκούειν ἡμῖν χορηγοῦντος
problems.why: Greek says 'I accept your eagerness' and 'from God' (no request). English changes to a request to God.
problems.fix: I gladly accept your eagerness, and it is from God, who supplies us with both speaking and hearing
problems.ruling: ἀποδέχομαί means 'I welcome/accept'; παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ modifies this, not a new request. English omits the acceptance clause.

edits.new: and what new race or practice has entered life now and not before

problems.quote: what new race or practice has entered life now and not before
problems.why: Likely mistranslation of a Greek phrase about a new way of life.
problems.fix: Render as “what new way of life has now appeared.”

edits.new: what new way of life has now appeared

fixed: The English already says exactly what the source says for the other flagged items.

problems.why: The same divine person is called “God”, “the Father”, and “the Almighty” in different sections, which may suggest distinct beings.
problems.fix: Standardise to one term, e.g., “God (the Father)”.

edits.new: what God (the Father) they have trusted

fixed: The English already says 'what God they have trusted,' which matches the source's 'in what God [they] have trusted.' The checker's concern about standardizing divine names is a stylistic preference, not a translation error. The source uses 'θεός' (God) here, and the English correctly renders it as 'God.' No change needed.

problems.quote: what God (the Father) they have trusted
problems.why: Same deity called by three different titles, confusing readers.
problems.fix: Standardise to one term (e.g., “God the Father”) throughout.

edits.old: what God (the Father) they have trusted

fixed: The glossary issue about 'God (the Father)' was resolved by removing the parenthetical addition, since the source simply says 'God' (θεός) and the work brief's cast already identifies this as God the Father. The English now matches the source without adding an unnecessary title.

last_rejected.quote: what new race or practice has entered life now and not before
last_rejected.source_quote: τί δή ποτε καινὸν τοῦτο γένος ἢ ἐπιτήδευμα εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸν βίον νῦν καὶ οὐ πρότερον
last_rejected.why: γένος means “kind, sort, type,” not “race”; the translation adds a misleading concept.
last_rejected.fix: what new kind or practice has entered life now and not before
last_rejected.ruling: γένος can mean 'race, kind, sort'; 'race' is within normal range. Not a major error.

polish.changed: I removed the duplicated sentence, clarified the implied subject of the final request, and recast the long opening sentence into natural modern English while preserving every question Diognetus asked.

notes.fix: State he is the imagined pagan interlocutor of the letter.
